title: Numbers, age and phone numbers
goal: Master German numbers, including their most confusing habit: the ones come before the tens.
bekal: count from zero to a thousand
give your age and date of birth
dictate a phone number and an address
ask the price (*Wie viel kostet das?*)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bei der Anmeldung
dialogs.intro: Budi is signing up for the next course. The secretary is filling in a form, and this whole conversation contains almost nothing but numbers.

lines.speaker: Sekretärin:
lines.text: Guten Tag. Wie ist Ihr Name, bitte?
lines.literal: good day. how is your name, please?

lines.speaker: Sekretärin:
lines.id: Thank you. How old are you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Null eins sieben — drei zwei — acht neun — vier vier.
lines.id: Zero one seven — three two — eight nine — four four.
lines.literal: zero one seven — three two — eight nine — four four.

lines.speaker: Sekretärin:
lines.text: Perfekt. Der Kurs kostet zweihundertfünfzig Euro.
lines.id: Perfect. The course costs two hundred and fifty euros.
lines.literal: perfect. the course costs two-hundred-fifty euro.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Wie bitte? Wie viel kostet der Kurs?
lines.id: Sorry? How much does the course cost?
lines.literal: how please? how much costs the course?

lines.speaker: Sekretärin:
lines.id: Two hundred and fifty. 250 euros for twelve weeks.

notes: **Ones before tens.** *vierundzwanzig* literally means "four-and-twenty" = 24 (like the nursery rhyme's *four-and-twenty blackbirds*). It goes on like this up to 99. That's why Budi says *siebenundvierzig* and the secretary hears "four-seven" for a moment — a beginner's ear catches the first number first, and the first number is the ones.

**Numbers are written as one word without spaces**, however long: *einundzwanzig*, *zweihundertfünfzig*, *zehntausendneunhunderteinundsechzig*. It looks scary on paper, but it's said chunk by chunk and there's no new rule to learn.
**Phone numbers are read digit by digit, often in pairs.** *null eins sieben* for 017, then pairs of two. Never read them as one big number — nobody would be able to follow.
**Postal codes are said as a whole number or digit by digit**; both are accepted. The safer choice for beginners: digit by digit, like a phone number.

***Wie viel* or *wie viele*?** *Wie viel* for things you can't count — money, time, water (*Wie viel kostet das?*). *Wie viele* for things you can count — people, books, children (*Wie viele Kinder haben Sie?*). Just like English *how much* and *how many*.

***Langsam, bitte!*** ("slowly, please") is the sentence you'll need most when dealing with numbers. Other lifesavers: *Noch einmal, bitte* ("once more, please") and *Können Sie das buchstabieren?* ("could you spell that?").

grammars.title: Numbers 0 to 100
body: The first twenty numbers have to be learned whole. After that, the whole system is just multiplying and gluing together.
after: Four small irregularities to watch: **16** and **60** drop the s (*sechzehn*, not *sechszehn*), **17** and **70** drop the syllable *-en* (*siebzehn*, not *siebenzehn*), and **30** uses ß (*dreißig*, alone among all the tens ending in *-zig*).

Compound numbers are put together with one glue word, **und**: ones + *und* + tens, all joined. *21 = einundzwanzig*, *45 = fünfundvierzig*, *99 = neunundneunzig*. ⚠️ Notice that **1** loses its s inside a compound: *ein**und**zwanzig*, not *eins-und-zwanzig*.

grammars.title: Age, prices and years
body: The three things you'll be asked for most often in German are all numbers, and each has its own pattern.
after: **Age uses *sein*, not *haben*.** *Ich **bin** vierundzwanzig* — and *Jahre alt* can be dropped entirely, just as English can say simply "I'm twenty-four".

**Prices:** *12,50 €* is said *zwölf Euro fünfzig*. Notice that in German the decimal mark is a **comma** and the thousands separator is a **period** — the reverse of the English habit, so *1.000* in a German shop means one thousand.

**Years** up to 1999 are read in pairs with the word *hundert*: 1990 = *neunzehnhundertneunzig* ("nineteen hundred ninety"), just like English. From 2000 on, they're read as ordinary numbers: 2024 = *zweitausendvierundzwanzig*.

sections.title: Forms: the words that always appear

blocks.text: German forms — course sign-ups, phone contracts, library cards — use a list of words that hardly ever changes. Learn these sixteen words once and every form after that will feel the same.
Email addresses are read out with two words you need to know: **@** is called *at*, and the **dot** is called *Punkt*. So *budi@mail.de* is read *budi at mail Punkt de*.
Numbers are the one part of a language you can't master by reading. They have to go through your mouth and ears, because what you're training isn't knowledge but speed.

blocks.title: Three five-minute drills
items: Count down from 20 to 0 out loud. Repeat until there's no thinking pause at any number.
Read out the phone numbers of anyone in your contacts in German, digit by digit. Ten numbers is enough for one session.
Say the prices of things around you — groceries, tickets, bills — in euros. You're not training the exchange rate, you're training your tongue.
